https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: 1:04 Mourners hold funeral for 112 people killed in 2023 by Israeli strike in Gaza – video Gaza Mass funeral held in Gaza for victims of 2023 Israeli strike Remains of 112 victims, including 40 children, recovered from rubble more than two years after residential block was destroyed William Christou Tue 4 Aug 2026 13.24 EDT Last modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 14.23 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Mourners gathered in central Gaza on Tuesday for a mass funeral for 112 people, including 40 children, who were killed in 2023 in one of the deadliest Israeli strikes of the Gaza war. Their bodies could not be recovered until now because of Israel’s continuing strikes, which have slowed, though not halted, since the ceasefire in October. Hundreds of people gathered around more than 100 coffins wrapped in Palestinian flags and arranged in rows on the ground in Deir al-Balah. Mourners prayed for the victims before carrying the bodies through rubble-lined streets and past destroyed buildings for burial in a nearby cemetery. The victims had been among more than 300 people killed on 22 November 2023, when Israeli warplanes demolished a residential block in Gaza City. The bodies of only about 40 people could be recovered by people at the scene, who dug through smouldering rubble with their bare hands and basic tools. Last weekend, Gaza’s civil defence dug through the levelled apartment block and recovered the remains of a further 112 victims, including women and children. It said 157 people were still missing after the attack. The ceasefire that was established in October – which has not stopped Israeli bombing of Gaza – has allowed first responders to dig through the rubble where thousands of remains are still buried across the territory. View image in fullscreen Palestinians carry the bodies through the rubble-lined streets of Deir al-Balah for burial in a nearby cemetery. Photograph: Mohammed Saber/EPA At least 7,400 people have been reported by relatives as still buried under the rubble, Zaher al-Waheidi, head of the Gaza health ministry’s records department, told the Associated Press. He added that the true number was probably thousands higher because some strikes had killed entire families, leaving no loved ones to report them missing. A UN commission, Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International have found that Israel committed genocide in Gaza. In June, a UN commission found that Israel was continuing to commit genocide in Gaza and that its security forces “deliberately targeted and killed” Palestinian children. At least 26 Palestinians were killed by Israeli strikes over the weekend, despite the announcement of a deal intended to solidify the second phase of the October ceasefire. The killings happened just a few days after the US president, Donald Trump, hailed the latest deal – intended to lead to Hamas disarming and Israeli troops withdrawing from Gaza – as a “historic agreement”. More than 73,000 people in Gaza have been killed by Israel since 7 October 2023, including more than 1,250 people since the October ceasefire. Israel launched the war in Gaza after a Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023 in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken hostage. Five Israeli soldiers have been killed since the October ceasefire. Ceasefire talks intended to move the agreement into a second phase have largely stalled. Senior Hamas officials said that the group’s disarmament is conditional on Israel withdrawing from the strip. Israel said that it had “serious security concerns” about last week’s agreement. Most of the Gaza Strip remains in ruins, with the vast majority of its 2 million population displaced and living through a humanitarian crisis in unsanitary, overcrowded tent cities. [Jiwan Kim, Edaily Reporter] Investor sentiment across South Korea's pharmaceutical and life sciences sectors remained weak on July 22 following the Phase 3 setback for Kolon TissueGene's osteoarthritis candidate TG-C. Kolon TissueGene hit the daily lower limit for a second consecutive session, while affiliate Kolon Life Science plunged 17%. The life sciences sector fell 3.48%, the steepest decline among all industry groups. The pharmaceutical sector closed 0.56% lower. Of its 160 listed companies, only 44 advanced, while 98 declined and 18 finished unchanged. In the life sciences sector, 36 of 91 stocks rose, 47 fell and eight ended flat. NanoEnTek Hits Upper Limit on Additional FDA Clearance NanoEnTek surged to the daily upper limit after securing additional clearance from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for its hematopoietic stem cell counter. According to KG Zeroin's MP Doctor, NanoEnTek closed at 4,540 won, up 1,045 won, or 29.90%, from the previous session. The company said its ADAM II-CD34 system received FDA clearance for use with cryopreserved hematopoietic progenitor cell-apheresis products, known as cryopreserved HPC-A. NanoEnTek website. (Screenshot by Jiwan Kim) The device had already been cleared for peripheral blood and cord blood testing. The additional indication allows major specimens used in hematopoietic stem cell transplantation to be analyzed with a single instrument. The latest approval brings NanoEnTek's total number of FDA 510(k)-cleared in-vitro diagnostic products to 13, which the company says is the highest among South Korean immunodiagnostic companies. Cryopreserved HPC-A is used in autologous stem cell transplantation for blood cancer patients. Stem cells are collected and frozen before high-dose chemotherapy, then tested for cell count and viability before being reinfused into the patient. The company said the expanded indication enables ADAM II-CD34 to be used in a critical quality-control stage of the autologous transplantation process. NanoEnTek also expects its recurring consumables business to benefit from a larger installed equipment base. Consumables for its in-vitro diagnostics and life sciences businesses accounted for 77.8% of total sales last year. Its high-throughput cell analysis platform, the EVE-HT series, is currently used by more than 30 global pharmaceutical and biotechnology companies. NanoEnTek estimates that cumulative consumables revenue can reach a level similar to the equipment sales price within about three years of installation. A company official said, "The FDA clearance has expanded the clinical application of ADAM II-CD34 and positioned it as a core quality-control instrument in the autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation process for blood cancer patients." The official added, "We will expand the presence of the ADAM series not only at blood cancer transplant centers in North America and Europe, but also in the Middle East, where demand for treatment of hereditary blood disorders is high." NGeneBio Jumps on Expansion of Blood Cancer Diagnostic Network NGeneBio also hit the daily upper limit as investors welcomed the expansion of its blood cancer precision diagnostic panel business. The shares closed at 2,370 won, up 545 won, or 29.86%, from the previous session. The rally followed news that NGeneBio had begun supplying its HEMAccuTest blood cancer panel to Seoul National University Bundang Hospital. The company currently supplies the panel to about 20 major tertiary hospitals in South Korea, including Seoul St. Mary's Hospital and Seoul National University Hospital. Overseas, it has expanded into Singapore, Vietnam, Colombia, Germany and Romania. NGeneBio's blood cancer panel business has posted a compound annual growth rate of 36% over the past five years. In the first quarter, domestic sales rose 38% from a year earlier, while overseas sales increased 102%. NGeneBio logo. (Courtesy of NGeneBio) HEMAccuTest analyzes major genetic mutations at the initial diagnosis stage. After treatment, the company's MRDaccuPanel AML FLT3 is used to monitor measurable residual disease and detect possible recurrence. The panel is designed to identify FLT3 mutations, a major biomarker in acute myeloid leukemia, at levels as low as 0.001%. The company said this sensitivity meets the ultra-high-sensitivity assessment requirements recommended by the European LeukemiaNet. NGeneBio is also seeking to use its blood cancer panels as companion diagnostic and biomarker platforms in drug development. Potential applications include selecting patients for FLT3-targeted therapies, evaluating treatment response and monitoring recurrence. Song Myung-jun, head of NGeneBio's diagnostics business, said, "The supply agreement with Seoul National University Bundang Hospital will further strengthen the clinical credibility and practical applicability of NGeneBio's blood cancer panels." He added, "We will expand our position in the precision blood cancer diagnostics market by increasing supplies to major domestic hospitals and securing additional global references." Kangstem, Extends Rally on Big Pharma Organoid Deal Kangstem Biotech continued to rise after signing a material transfer and evaluation agreement, or MTEA, with a global top-five pharmaceutical company. Kang Kyung-sun, founder of Kangstem Biotech and professor at Seoul National University. (Photo courtesy of Kangstem Biotech) The shares gained 145 won, or 6.89%, to close at 2,250 won. Under the agreement, the partner will apply its drug candidates to Kangstem Biotech's hair follicle organoid platform to evaluate efficacy. The goal is to obtain data that may predict clinical outcomes more accurately than conventional animal testing. The company described the contract as the first stage of a strategic partnership that could potentially expand into joint research, research service agreements or licensing deals. Kangstem Biotech's organoid platform uses human-derived tissue to mimic the structure and function of actual organs. It is designed to assess complex cellular responses that are difficult to reproduce using conventional artificial skin models. The company also sees potential applications in transplantable products for hair loss and skin disease treatments. Kangstem Biotech founder Kang Kyung-sun, a professor at Seoul National University. (Courtesy of Kangstem Biotech) Leading Investment & Securities said the agreement demonstrated the global commercial potential of Kangstem Biotech's Real Skin Organoid technology. The brokerage noted that the pharmaceutical partner will test drug candidates using the hair follicle organoid platform, potentially generating data with stronger clinical predictability than animal studies. It added that positive evaluation results could lead to shorter development timelines, improved clinical success rates and follow-on collaboration, including licensing or joint development. Kang Kyung-sun, founder of Kangstem Biotech and a professor at Seoul National University, said six research and business development executives from the multinational pharmaceutical company visited Kangstem Biotech's research facility in May. "It was highly unusual for them to review not only our core organoid technology but also our production capabilities at a level comparable to technical due diligence," Kang said. Photograph: Mark Nelson Immigration and asylum Man under threat of deportation to Jamaica wins right to rejoin his British family Mark Nelson released from immigration detention on bail after lawyers challenge decision to remove him Diane Taylor Sun 16 Aug 2026 07.27 EDT Last modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 07.28 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A Jamaican man who has lived more than half his life in the UK and was facing imminent deportation has been allowed to reunite with his British family after a legal challenge. Mark Nelson, 47, came to the UK in 2000 and later set up his own car-mechanic business. He has five British children and a British partner. He faced deportation in 2022 after serving a four-year prison sentence for possession with intent to supply a class B drug, abstracting electricity and two offences of racially aggravated intentional harassment. He had not committed any further offences. The deportation was later cancelled and instead he was tagged and told to report weekly at a Home Office centre. But last month – almost 10 years after his original conviction – Nelson was arrested, detained and told that the government again planned to deport him to Jamaica. The Home Office gave him a ticket for a flight on 7 August, but after reading about his case in the Guardian , lawyers offered to represent him pro bono to challenge his deportation. After they made an 11th-hour application for a judicial review the Home Office backed down on the deportation and cancelled his ticket. This week he was granted bail and can return to the home he shares with his partner, Rachel Derbyshire, in the north of England and see his children again. Nelson said he was overjoyed to to have left the immigration detention centre near Heathrow where he had spent several weeks in hot and crowded conditions. “I’ve spoken to my kids, my partner and my brother,” he said. “Everyone is so excited about my release. If it hadn’t been for the lawyers who got in touch after reading the Guardian article I would be back in Jamaica by now, separated from my family, not knowing when I would see them again. “I have no family members there and believe my life would be at risk.” Naga Kandiah of MTC Solicitors, who contacted Nelson after reading about his case, lodged the judicial review application. He has also lodged an appeal relating to his immigration case in the first-tier tribunal and a referral has been made for him to the national referral mechanism as a potential victim of modern slavery. Kandiah said: “He committed his offences in 2017 and served his sentence. Yet nearly a decade later he continues to endure the threat of deportation, with the devastating possibility that he could be permanently torn away from his British children and partner. A prison sentence should not become a life sentence by another name. “Vulnerable people can struggle to secure legal representation when they need it most. When a person facing removal cannot access timely legal advice, the risk is that the Home Office can remove them before their case has been properly scrutinised.” Nelson wrote an opinion piece for the Guardian in 2022 about being under threat of deportation. He said Jamaica was a place where he no longer knew anyone after his great-grandparents, who brought him up there, died when he was 16. A Home Office spokesperson said: “All foreign national offenders who receive a prison sentence in the UK are referred for deportation at the earliest opportunity. “We have removed or deported almost 70,000 people who were here illegally since the last election, an increase of 41%.” Explore more on these topics Immigration and asylum Home Office Jamaica Commonwealth immigration Caribbean news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland

Photograph: Erin Hooley/AP View image in fullscreen Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents make an arrest. Photograph: Erin Hooley/AP First Thing newsletter US news First Thing: ‘Third country’ deportation can resume, US supreme court rules Trump administration can deport immigrants to countries other than their homeland. Plus, 550lb bear returns to LA neighborhood Martin Belam Wed 30 Sep 2026 07.18 EDT Last modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 07.37 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Good morning. The supreme court has ruled the Trump administration can resume deporting immigrants to “third countries” , or countries other than their homeland, without giving them any opportunity to contest their removals. The six-justice conservative majority of the high court temporarily lifted a decision by a lower court that required the administration to provide immigrants sufficient notice and the opportunity to claim fear of torture or persecution in the countries where they were being sent. What has the administration asked the supreme court to rule on about trans prisoners? The administration asked the justices to allow it to deny gender-affirming care to transgender people in federal prisons. The solicitor general, D John Sauer, wrote that gender-reassignment surgeries, hormone therapy and social accommodations such as undergarments, makeup, padding and wigs “could no longer be justified.” Why is the EPA union suing the administration? The union, which represents more than 8,000 workers at the Environmental Protection Agency, has filed a lawsuit against the EPA and the agency’s administrator, Lee Zeldin, alleging it illegally terminated a collective bargaining agreement. Which legal battle has Trump appeared to have conceded? The president has agreed to stop fighting the disbursement of E Jean Carroll’s $5m verdict in her 2023 sexual abuse and defamation civil trial against him, a procedural development as the funds had already been distributed to her. Trump announces vague ‘morally binding’ AI deal among tech CEOs for ‘tremendous self-policing’ View image in fullscreen Donald Trump also signed an executive order renaming artificial intelligence as ‘superintelligence’. Photograph: Tierney L Cross/UPI/Shutterstock Donald Trump announced Tuesday that the heads of the largest US tech and AI companies had signed on to a “morally binding” agreement to put controls on artificial intelligence. He announced the deal after a White House lunch with top tech executives. The agreement, which Trump suggested would allow the companies to perform “tremendous self-policing” of their products and technologies, outlines a vague framework for how AI firms would establish safety standards. Trump also signed an executive order renaming artificial intelligence to “superintelligence”, similar to a declaration he made at the UN last week. What new product has OpenAI announced? Less than 24 hours after OpenAI said it would scrap the launch of a model over safety concerns, the company debuted a whole new suite of artificial intelligence tools , including “dots”, agents it said were “more ambitious” than ChatGPT and a “whole new way to work with AI.” Why is Greta Garbo making AI headlines? More than a century after her screen debut and decades after she was laid to rest, the actor has been reanimated by AI for a Swedish advert. Peter Bradshaw has given it a damning one-star review . US Senate blocks resolution demanding accountability over Israeli violence in West Bank View image in fullscreen Israeli settlers attacking Palestinians near the West Bank settlement of Bat Ayin. Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum The US Senate rejected along mostly party lines a Democratic resolution that would have forced the state department to report to Congress on violence in the occupied West Bank, including the killings of nine American citizens by Israeli settlers or security forces over the last few years. Why did an Israeli-bound plane make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia? A passenger jet travelling from Dubai made an emergency landing, briefly raising concerns about a possible hijacking and prompting Israel to scramble warplanes. Reports said the incident stemmed from a feud between the plane’s two pilots , and everyone onboard was safe. What has Zohran Mamdani announced about antisemitism? The New York City mayor has debuted a sweeping plan to combat antisemitism . The strategy includes increased security funding for synagogues and an increased focus on incorporating Jewish history into public school education. The plan is seen as a move to assuage critics who see his steadfast denunciations of Israel as antisemitic. Why are two authors suing the city of Los Angeles? Jenan Matari, a Palestinian-American author, and Nora Lester Murad, a Jewish-American writer, are taking the action after public library officials scrapped their Read Palestine Week book talks. Texts about alleged Cornell gang-rape released after investigation reopened View image in fullscreen Only two of the alleged seven perpetrators were subsequently expelled after an internal investigation by Cornell University. Photograph: Heather Ainsworth/AP Excerpts of text messages reportedly exchanged by a defendant in the Cornell University gang-rape case and the woman who claimed she was assaulted were published by CBS News on Tuesday , a day after New York prosecutors said they were reopening a criminal investigation. Two of the alleged perpetrators were subsequently expelled after an internal investigation by Cornell – while the other five were allowed to resume their studies at the Ivy League institution after writing an essay, attending a workshop, or serving a short suspension. None were ever arrested or charged. In other news … View image in fullscreen The machinations of the Lindsay Clancy case has gripped the US. Photograph: Greg Derr/Pool The Patriot Ledger/AP Lindsay Clancy returns to court as lawyer asks judge to find her not guilty . The office of the Plymouth country district attorney again chose to not disclose whether it plans to try Clancy again. A team of skydivers dropped in to help survivors of a plane crash in Wisconsin , using their training as paramedics to treat victims before ground crews arrived. A Brazilian news site has said it will not cover upcoming elections after threats. The independent Tapajós de Fato said decision was made to protect journalists and their families. The nor’easter storm that pummeled New England looks to have exposed large segments of a 19th-century schooner shipwrecked in the so-called graveyard of the Atlantic. No 8 seeds Liberty sprung a historic WNBA playoff upset to take down No 1 seeds Lynx. New York now await the winner of the Atlanta-Washington series Stat of the day: Judge ends federal oversight of Oakland police department after 23 years View image in fullscreen An officer with the Oakland police department. Photograph: Jeff Chiu/AP In the early 2000s, a group of police officers known as the “riders” were exposed for offenses such as planting evidence, falsifying reports and using excessive force against primarily young Black men. As part of a settlement of these cases, OPD was put on a federal court-ordered reform program , which has now ended. Well Actually: Does GLP-1 use result in significant hair loss? View image in fullscreen The side-effect of the weight-loss drug is getting more attention from researchers. Composite: The Guardian/Getty Images Experts share what you need to know about GLP-1-related hair loss as the side-effect gets more attention from researchers . Don’t miss this: Three deaths, three states, 24 hours: one day in ICE’s quiet but ‘gruesome’ surge View image in fullscreen José Olivares examines the cases of three men who became the latest casualties of Trump’s anti-immigration campaign. Composite: Rita Liu/The Guardian/Getty Images/GoFundMe In the latest in our ICE investigation, José Olivares examines the cases of three men who became casualties in the latest phase of Trump’s anti-immigration campaign. … or this: The secret lives of men who read romance books View image in fullscreen Many heterosexual men are sharing their reading passions in forums online. Illustration: Laurie Avon/The Guardian It is often assumed straight men are not interested in romantic fiction – but, as Amandas Ong discovers , many are sharing their passion in forums online. Climate check: Antarctic winter sea ice falls to third-lowest level on record as scientists warn of ‘now problem’ View image in fullscreen The four lowest years on record for Antartica’s sea ice have occurred in the last four years. Photograph: Peace Portal Photo/Alamy Antarctica’s winter sea ice has peaked at its third-lowest level on record , scientists have confirmed. The four lowest years on record for the continent’s sea ice – a vital component of the planet’s climate and critical for marine life – have all occurred in the last four years. Photograph: Jae C Hong/AP Bless him, the 550lb bear made famous after he took up residence under an Altadena home in November 2025 is wandering the same Los Angeles neighborhood again . https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: Pictures on a blackened wall in Nir Oz commemorate victims of the 7 October attacks. The sign says Benjamin Netanyahu has blood on his hands. Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Pictures on a blackened wall in Nir Oz commemorate victims of the 7 October attacks. The sign says Benjamin Netanyahu has blood on his hands. Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The Guardian Israel ‘All I want to do is cry’: trauma of 7 October survivors three years after the attacks Israeli communities shattered by Hamas massacres are torn between rebuilding their lives and remembering lost friends and relatives Emma Graham-Harrison and Quique Kierszenbaum in Nir Oz Tue 6 Oct 2026 16.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 17.26 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google K eith Siegel spent many of his long hours in Hamas captivity in Gaza etching everything that happened after 7 October 2023 into his memory. For 484 days, he recited to himself every place he was held, the dates he was moved and every attack or humiliation he endured or witnessed. He aimed to store intelligence that could help Israeli forces free other hostages if he was released, to keep track of time as the days slid by and be able to tell his family what happened to him. Now his body is free, but he cannot loosen those memories. “I’m living a kind of dual life,” he said in an interview in Tel Aviv. “I’m here for some of the time, and I’m in Gaza some of time. It’s very challenging to convey in words what it was like.” View image in fullscreen Aviva and Keith Siegel were abducted from their home in Kfar Aza in southern Israel by Hamas on 7 October 2023. Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The Guardian Siegel and his wife, Aviva, were among 251 people taken captive to Gaza on the deadliest day in Israel’s history, when Hamas militants broke across the border to launch a wave of attacks on kibbutzim, border towns, military bases and music festivals. Israel’s security forces were caught by surprise, and by the time they regained control of the area, 1,209 people had been killed, the majority of them civilians, including 36 children, according to records kept by the Israeli newspaper Haaretz. The cemetery at Nir Oz contains two lines of fresh headstones, marking lives that all ended on that same date. A shared plot for a family of five – a mother, father and their three young children – has been made into a garden with space left for their still-living grandparents. Caretaker Shlomo Margalit, who will soon turn 89, points to the graves of three of his oldest friends, founding members of the kibbutz who came to Nir Oz from Haifa with him in the 1950s. “This is my life project, as well as my home,” Margalit said, explaining why he has come back to a place of such loss. He is waiting for a new house but, for now, staying in the former home of Gadi Moses, 82, who survived 482 days as a hostage. View image in fullscreen Shlomo Margalit, a founder of Kibbutz Nir Oz, survived the Hamas attack in his safe room together with his wife, Hanna. Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The Guardian The graves he tends are a silent testament to the brutality of the attacks and the scale of the state’s failure, which in Nir Oz was staggering, even on a day of terrible failures. A five-person volunteer defence force held Hamas at bay for at least two hours, Margalit said. When they had all been shot, the kibbutz was taken over and sacked, homes burned, families slaughtered and kidnapped. Then, before the first Israeli soldier arrived, the Hamas forces, other Palestinian gunmen and civilian looters all left. Nir Oz had been forgotten by the army and ripped apart without the military firing a single shot to defend it. In total, 47 people were killed and 76 taken to Gaza, including Shiri Bibas , her 10-month-old baby Kfir and four-year-old Ariel, who were killed in Gaza. The dead and hostages represented more than a quarter of the small community. View image in fullscreen Shlomo Margalit tends to the graves in the Nir Oz cemetery, a silent testimony to the 7 October attacks. Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The Guardian Revisiting that terrible day, and the trauma that followed, is painful and exhausting for Margalit, but he still accepts interviews for a simple reason. “I want people to know what really happened here,” the 89-year-old said. The third anniversary of the 7 October attacks falls a few weeks before national elections, and much of the country is caught up in a furious debate about responsibility for the deadliest day in Israel’s history and the conduct of the war that followed. Survivors and bereaved relatives are avoiding the political fray, still grappling with the trauma and the struggle to rebuild something like normality. In Nir Oz, there is a terrible, almost irreconcilable struggle between re-establishing the kibbutz as a living community, and preserving physical testimony of the attack. Freed Israeli hostage Aviva Siegel on Netanyahu’s unbearable strategy and waiting for her husband to come home Read more The cemetery echoes with the sound of construction and families have already moved into several rows of new houses near the kibbutz entrance. But on the other side of the compound, paths still lead between blackened ruins and memorials to the dead. Some bereaved survivors want the homes of loved ones preserved this way as permanent monuments to mark their loss. “There are families that can’t [bear to] live here, but want a memorial place to come to visit,” Margalit said. “On the other hand, can you build a new kibbutz where children grow up running around between burnt houses?” He is on the remembrance committee and, two years on, they are struggling to reach a decision on this impossible choice. “Is there right or wrong here? No,” he said. “We are dealing with that, trying to find an answer.” One compromise might be a memorial garden on the border of the kibbutz. For now, there are plaques with the stories of families attacked on that day and a memorial house to remember the dead and kidnapped. When the kibbutz took a collective decision to return and rebuild, Margalit and his wife, Hanna, knew they wanted to join. His only concession to the trauma was asking for a new home that did not face Gaza. View image in fullscreen About 60% of the houses in Nir Oz were destroyed on 7 October and some families have decided not to return. Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The Guardian “I’ve found myself building this place for the second time,” he said. “I know when I’m gone, I will have done something with my life. I took part in putting this spot on the map.” The Siegels, who lived in the nearby kibbutz of Kfar Aza, also among the worst hit, have decided not to return as they focus on mental and physical recovery. Aviva was 62 when she was kidnapped. Keith was 64. “ What happened to me in Gaza, what happened with Keith in Gaza, it’s there all the time,” said Aviva. “I understand that it’s going to be a process of healing. There’s always things that remind me, and if I don’t remember, then he reminds me. If I’m cooking lunch or making a cup of tea and I turn around and see Keith with tears in his eyes, because he just read something or let himself feel.” The days approaching the anniversary have been particularly difficult, she said. Last year, at this time, she was still campaigning for the release of other hostages, her own emotions held at bay by the urgency of that campaign. For a time, she tried to deal with the trauma by telling herself, over and over again “I must feel lucky,” simply because she had made it back alive. Now she has allowed herself to feel again, and as 7 October approached, she has realised how raw the wounds still are. “Getting ready [for the anniversary] has been very very painful,” she said. “The last couple of weeks all I want to do is cry. Now I’m feeling things I didn’t feel before.” View image in fullscreen Aviva Siegel has written a book about her ordeal, saying it was therapy and an act of celebration. Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The Guardian “When I hear my grandson say he is afraid of being kidnapped in the middle of the night, it breaks my heart.” She has written a book, Survived to Tell , about the ordeal, which she describes as therapy and an act of celebration. She wrote so her grandchildren could read about what she and Keith endured, for other hostages who couldn’t tell their own stories and to inspire a broader audience in Israel and beyond. After the exhausting campaign to get Keith and other hostages home, she said she had struggled to concentrate on the election. Keith’s political focus is an independent inquiry into 7 October to prevent other families suffering as his has. He said: “There needs to be an investigation to understand how this happened, in order to do everything possible that it won’t happen again. So many people were killed, injured, traumatised.” Benjamin Netanyahu, the prime minister, has fiercely opposed an independent state commission of inquiry. Critics say he is afraid it would expose his own failings. In the immediate aftermath of the attacks, few people inside or outside Israel expected him to stay in power long, particularly as the country’s coalition governments have rarely served out their full terms. Netanyahu had for years championed a foreign and security policy based on the premise that Hamas was “contained” in Gaza, behind unbreachable layers of fortifications. The security officials who were in command that day have all stepped down yet, three years on, Netanyahu is still in power, having deflected all demands for his resignation. Yaakov Godo, a bereaved father, interrupted Netanyahu’s speech at the official commemoration event this year to accuse him of negligence. “You did not protect my son on 7 October, you did not protect 1,200 people murdered in one day. Shame!” he shouted, before being ushered away. View image in fullscreen The back of Yocheved Lifshitz’s home in Nir Oz. She has become a vocal critic of Benjamin Netanyahu. Photograph: The Guardian Both US and Israeli officials have said Netanyahu rejected ceasefire deals that could have halted the war in Gaza and brought many Israeli hostages home sooner. But criticising the prime minister means venturing into a vicious political debate where age and loss offer little protection. Yocheved Lifshitz, 88, was taken hostage from Nir Oz with her husband Oded, whose magnificent cactus garden blooms at the heart of the kibbutz. He died in Gaza, she survived and since her return she has been a vocal critic of Netanyahu. A candidate for Netanyahu’s Likud party, Itzik Bonzel, said last month that he wished he could turn back the clock and return her to Hamas captivity. He later apologised, blaming grief for his son who died fighting in Gaza, but Lifshitz denounced it as a proxy attack driven by the prime minister. Netanyahu, who is battling a corruption trial and could be more vulnerable legally if he loses power, is pushing to intensify Israeli attacks on Gaza and his coalition partners are calling for ethnic cleansing and annexation of Palestine . View image in fullscreen The graves of Oded Lifshitz and Alex (Alexander) Dancyg, who were abducted by Hamas on 7 October. Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The Guardian The war Israel launched in response to 7 October has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, the majority of them civilians, including about 20,000 children. Netanyahu has also waged a years-long campaign to dismantle institutions protecting democracy inside Israel’s 1967 borders. Palestinians under Israeli military rule in the occupied West Bank do not have the rights of Israeli citizens. Many Israelis opposed to this rightwing vision of perpetual war in a state with diminished institutions consider this election the most critical since Israel was founded in 1948, among them Margalit. Nir Oz, like many communities targeted by Hamas, had its roots in the leftwing Zionist movement, and although the brutality of 7 October pushed some to the right, others saw their pain as bitter proof that war alone cannot offer long-term security. “I don’t believe we can ignore the fact that Palestinians live here,” Margalit said. “We have to find a way we can live here with them and be secure. I don’t have an answer, I just know we are here to stay and they are here to stay. Maybe we need someone from the outside.” Explore more on these topics Israel Gaza Palestine Benjamin Netanyahu Middle East and north Africa news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness
